description: Team Sitara OPS is Shreya Saxena, building solo. In August 2023, wildfire forced me out of my home in Kelowna. That night, maps showed where the fire was, but nothing could tell me if this was normal. This challenge was that exact question. Over the weekend I built Ember alone: the data pipeline, the harmonization model and its validation, the web app, the design and the mascot guide. One consistent record of Canadian fire, 2000 to today. Satellites die. Their memory shouldn’t.
summary: In August 2023, wildfire forced me out of my home in Kelowna. I left not knowing if I’d have a home to come back to. That night I kept looking for embers. Maps showed where it was burning. Nothing could tell me what it meant: had this valley ever burned like this, and was the worst still coming? NASA has watched fire from space for 26 years, but that memory is split in two. VIIRS (since 2012) finds about four times as many fire cell-days as MODIS (since 2000) in the same fires, so the raw record jumps fourfold in 2012, and any trend across it measures a change of satellite, not a change in fire. And the satellites carrying MODIS, Terra and Aqua, are ending in 2027. Ember joins the record. It puts every NASA FIRMS archive hotspot over Canada on one VIIRS scale, using ratios learned where both sensors overlap, by ecozone, land cover, season and fire intensity. Draw a box anywhere in Canada and Ember shows its burning calendar: which months burn, which years were worst, how this month compares with the historical median, and where fire is rising or falling. Beyond that: live hotspots, people in the fire’s path, likely ranges on estimated years, CSV downloads, colour-blind-friendly scales, and an Ember mascot that tours the app. Emergency responders can see when to stage crews, firefighters whether a season is running hot, land managers where fire regimes are shifting, and scientists can finally draw trends from 2000 to today. Satellites die. Their memory shouldn’t.
details:
Github link: https://github.com/6s-1/modis-viirs-fire-harmonisation

This project won 2nd Runner up for Local Impact Award at Toronto Local Event Nasa Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Why I built this
In August 2023, wildfire forced me out of my home in Kelowna, BC. That night I kept looking for embers. The maps could show me where the fire was. Nothing could tell me what it meant: had this valley ever burned like this, and was the worst still coming? The answer exists. NASA satellites have recorded every fire hotspot on Earth for 26 years. But that record is split in two. Ember is the tool I wish I’d had that night.

The problem
MODIS (since 2000) is the long memory: 26 years of fire. VIIRS (since 2012) is the sharper eye, with 375 m pixels against MODIS’s 1 km. In the same fires, VIIRS records about 4.3 times as many fire cell-days as MODIS. Put the records end to end and fire appears to jump fourfold in 2012, the year VIIRS arrived. Nothing on the ground changed; only the satellite did. Any trend drawn across 2012 measures that switch, not a change in fire. Planners budget crews against a false “normal”, insurers price risk from a false upward trend, and researchers must throw away half the history. The only way to translate MODIS into VIIRS is to learn from the years both were flying.

What Ember does
Ember turns every NASA FIRMS hotspot over Canada since November 2000 into one consistent record. Draw a box anywhere in Canada and Ember shows:

  • Burning-activity calendar: every month since 2000, with estimated months flagged.
  • Anomalies: this month compared with the historical median.
  • Trends: where fire is significantly rising or falling.
  • Season timing: when each year’s season started, peaked and ended.
  • Why it burned: fire causes, hectares burned, land cover.
  • Live fire: NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 hotspots compared with the same days in past years.
  • People: population in the area, and which fire areas expose the most people.
  • Downloads: CSV and PNG.
  • Guided tour: led by the Ember mascot.

How it works

  1. Clean: 12.5 million of 13.8 million FIRMS detections are kept. Only vegetation fires stay, and low-confidence detections are removed.
  2. One unit: a fire cell-day is one ~1 km hexagon where one satellite saw fire on one day.
  3. VIIRS reference: the mean of Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, with 60 outage days masked.
  4. Learn the conversion: for 2012–2025, Ember learns how many VIIRS cell-days match one MODIS cell-day, separately for each ecozone, land cover, season and fire-intensity group.
  5. Rebuild the past: 2000–2012 is rebuilt on the VIIRS scale. From 2012 on, the real observations are kept unchanged.

How I know it’s right
Nothing used to build the model was used to prove it.

  • I checked it against the day i was evacuated. I drew a box over Kelowna and went to August 2023. On the map I could find the cell where I was evacuated, lit up with fire. In the burn chart, the month I was evacuated stands out clearly. The data shows what I lived through.
  • Years the model never saw: with each year from 2012 to 2025 hidden in turn, Canada-wide yearly error is 5.7%, and 8.2% by province.

Who it helps

  • Emergency responders can stage crews and warn communities before a season peaks.
  • Firefighters can see whether a month is exceptional.
  • Land managers can see where fire regimes are shifting.
  • Scientists finally get trends from 2000 to today.
  • Communities get answers in seconds, with no GIS skills needed.

What makes it creative

  • Fire and people, side by side. Compare mode shows two globes locked together, fire on one and population on the other. Hover a place on either and the same spot lights up on both, so you can see at a glance where fire and people meet.
  • Live fire, read against history. Live hotspots are drawn in the same cells and colours as the 26-year record. Each live window is compared with the same days in past years, so “what’s burning now” comes with “is that unusual here?” built in.
  • Colour designed to be read by everyone. The fire scale darkens in even steps, so it reads the same in greyscale and with colour blindness. Anomalies use a purple-to-orange scale that stays distinct. Nothing depends on telling red from green.
  • A guide built in, not a manual. The Ember mascot is a demo widget that runs a guided tour for each mode. It spotlights the real controls one step at a time, so a first-time user is reading fire history in under a minute.
  • It explains, not just counts. The “Why it burned” card joins satellite fire with recorded causes, burned area, land cover and live agency status, so every number on the map comes with its story.
  • A new way to count fire. The fire cell-day makes satellites with 1 km and 375 m pixels count the same thing, and fire intensity fixes the hardest, most extreme years.

Factors I considered

  • Ease of first use: satellite fire data is hard to learn. Most tools assume GIS skills and leave new users stuck on an empty map. The Ember mascot’s guided tour solves that.
  • Accessibility: WCAG AA contrast, three text sizes, full keyboard use, screen-reader labels, reduced motion and colour-blind-friendly scales.
  • Honesty: estimated years are flagged with likely ranges, small areas get a low-confidence badge, and every number is read from pipeline files.
  • Security: the FIRMS key stays server-side.
  • Fairness across the map: an equal-area hexagon grid.

Limits

  • Extreme northern fire years are underestimated: 2014 reads 19.2% low.
  • 2001–2002 read low, and raw Terra shows the same gap.
  • Population is a single 2020 snapshot.
  • Canada only, for now.

Next

  • Test ML models such as gradient boosting against the current ratio tables, adding fire weather, fuel and terrain as inputs.
  • Add yearly population data, so exposure tracks where people lived each year.
  • Extend Ember to other countries.
  • Add smoke context.

Tools

  • Python: pandas, GeoPandas, rasterio, h3, SciPy.
  • JavaScript: Vite, MapLibre GL JS, h3-js.
  • A Cloudflare Worker, and GitHub Pages for hosting.
